en: *Amaraugha-prabodha* by Gorakṣanātha. (From Tirupati, Madras). Manuscript No. D-4339. Number of granthas: 125. Number of pages: 9. *Note: Input by James Mallinson, May 2008. Please send corrections to jim@khecari.com. Extracted from Mallik’s 1954 edition, which was based on a single manuscript.*

%Anything in round brackets is found in round brackets in the edition. Square brackets enclose my comments. %NB 32: cd is shared with AS and HP, but ab is shared only with HP; thus, AP is closer to HP than to AS?

There is a 55% mention of *śaktidhyāna*, but *kuṇḍalinī* is mentioned only once. Verse 31.5 states that there are two *haṭhayogas*: through the practice of *bindu* and *vāyu*. This text appears to describe the *vāyu* technique, which pierces the three *granthis*. Gorakṣa is mentioned three times. Oṃ, salutation be to Ādinātha; salutation indeed to Mīnanātha. Salutation to Caurāṅginātha, the wise one, perfected and awakened. (1) [Note: *caurāṅgi* is the emendation; the edition reads *cāraṅgi*.]

For those who have entered the stages beginning with *laya* and whose minds are eager for quarrel, Gorakṣaka has declared this awakening (*prabodha*) consisting of conviction (*pratyaya*). [2] Awakening;
*layayoga*, *haṭhayoga*, and *mantrayoga* as the third.

And the fourth is the Royal Yoga (*rājayoga*), which is free from the two-fold state of becoming. That which is the dissolution of the continuum of the mind is designated as *laya*; that which is intent upon obstructing the vital breath (*prabhañjana*) is *haṭha*. (3) *Prabhañjana* = wind; *pidhāna* = obstruction (emended by AGS; the edition reads *vidhāna*, following JB 2012).
That which is under the control of the form of mantra is mantra-yoga;
that which is devoid of mental fluctuations is rāja-yoga.
[4] Thus, rāja-yoga is sometimes said to be of two kinds: the medicinal (auṣadhya) and the internal (adhyātmaka).
Haṭha is also of two kinds; in some cases, it arises from the practice of the vital breath and the seminal drop. ||5||
This mantra, which is the cause for accomplishing the six activities, is not seen [externally];
like a worm within the eyebrows, nose, and so forth, the mind is somehow submerged [therein] and does not emerge.

The vital breath does not enter the foundation (ādhāra) of yogis through various kinds of practice, except through the illustrious Rājayoga, which consists of eternal bliss and is the abode of splendor. (6)
One who constantly mutters mantras does not obtain kingship, nor likewise sovereignty;
even union with a celestial woman is not attained daily by one who does not meditate.
"Tell me, O Lord, how can a horse be born from a female elephant, a young elephant from a donkey, or boiled rice from *kodrava* grain, by means of *haṭha* (force), without one’s own power?
Some drink foul urine; some eat saliva from their food.
Some, having entered the wood, lead the drop from the vulva of the young woman upward.
Some consume the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), their veins throughout the entire body becoming adept at the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*);
yet for them, there is no perfection of the body without this *rājayoga*, which transcends the individual mind. When the mind has attained equanimity, the vital air proceeds into the central channel.
This is known as Amarolī, Vajrolī, Tadāmatī, and Matā; thus Sahajolī is produced.
And likewise in the Śrīsampuṭa: "When the breath is forcefully restrained, there is a swallowing within the belly of the fish."
The Lord Kaivalya, having been suddenly liberated, remains so long as he does not perceive.
Having spoken thus, Giriśa said: "The time for this has not yet passed;
let us dwell eternally with Pārvatī, O Lord of Fishes. (10)
If one were to live by means of medicinal herbs in a world free from affliction, how could those physicians—who themselves are seized by old age and disease—ever die? (11)

How can there be the destruction of that [disease], which is expert in following the tracks of wandering physicians, possesses a restless intellect, is eager to hear from Suśruta, and for which the mind is the primary medicine? (12)
The two great medicines, *bindu* and *nāda*, exist within all living beings;
yet, failing to recognize them, everyone dies, deprived of a spiritual teacher. (13)
One should cause the concealed wind to move; it will milk forth the sun and fire.
Blazing, it moves from this [place], and because of that, O Pārvatī, the seed moves. 14.
For one who knows the essence of these two through the instruction of a true guru, whence can there be fear of physical suffering, old age, disease, evil, or death? (15)
When the King of Mind has emerged and the sun of harsh radiance travels along the path of Meru on all sides;
when the fire-nature is difficult to traverse and the moon flows forth, filling the body of the swift one;
when the fire is raised amidst a mass of bliss and the darkness of delusion—such as "this is yours" or "this is mine"—is abandoned.
When the aperture of Brahmā has burst open, there arises a certain unprecedented union of Śiva and Śivā—victory to that! ||16||
Indeed, there is only one multitude of immortals designated as the "King Yoga" (rājayoga).
How can a fourth [type], joined with *māyā* and the others, be given?
[Furthermore,] it is [divided into] the mild, the moderate, the inferior, and likewise the superior.
The practitioner is to be known as fourfold; that is here called the "staircase. ||18||

One who is of little enthusiasm, of dull passion, dependent on others, a jester, afflicted by disease, lacking in strength, a householder, and gentle is known as "mild" (mṛdu). One who possesses an even mind, practices with equanimity, has an even body, and an even basis [of support] is [known as "even" (sama)]. (19)
One who is neutral toward all undertakings is called a person of middling nature (*madhyasattva*).
One who is endowed with patience, vigor, and skillful means, who is mature, possessed of strength,
self-controlled, firm, and heroic, is declared to be of superior nature (*adhimātra*).
He has practiced all the treatises, is charming, and possesses vigor and heroism;
he is free from delusion, endowed with all perfections, changeless, and a great refuge. ||22||
Even that great body proceeds with even greater intensity;
they cross the ocean of existence and cause others to cross as well. (23)
To the mild, the mantra is given; to the middling, dissolution (laya) is taught;
to the intense, one should apply forceful effort (haṭha); [thus] the host of immortals [attains success] in Maheśvara.
Therein, the mantra is the single-syllable mantra "Ahaḥ," preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
Having meditated upon Śiva, the Auspicious One, in the heart within the twelfth divided maṇḍala. (25)
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one shall destroy even the most terrible death;
having performed the fire-oblation ten times the number of recitations with honey, milk, ghee, and lotuses. (26)
Now, regarding dissolution (laya):
He who meditates upon the god Śiva in Kāmarūpa, appearing like a linga and resembling a gem, dripping the essence of nectar into his own body; ||27||
Through continuous practice for six months, one shall attain perfection;
freed from wrinkles and grey hair, one shall live for three hundred years. (28)
Now, as for *haṭha*:
having pressed the vulva with the left foot and extended the right leg, one should fill the mouth with both hands. (29)
Having fixed the bond at the throat and drawn the vital air upward from its base,
the Kuṇḍalinī power suddenly becomes straightened, just as a snake struck by a staff becomes straight like a staff. (30)
Then that state of death arises, residing in the two petals (dvipuṭāśritā).
Great diseases, great afflictions, old age, death, and so forth are worn away;
therefore, the best of the wise call this Mahāmudrā.
That by which the great seal (mahāmudrā) is formed for the practitioner so that it may be accomplished is called the "Great Bond" (mahābandha), the destroyer of old age and death. ||33||
Having filled the mouth with air and placed the chin upon the heart,
one should firmly contract the *yoni* and fix the mind in the center.
This [practice] purifies the upward movement of all the channels.
Having brought about the confluence of the three channels (triveṇī), one should cause the mind to reach Kedāra.
Just as a woman endowed with beauty and grace is [useless] without a man,
so too the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) and the Great Lock (mahābandha) are fruitless when devoid of penetration (vedha).
One should firmly hold the extended left foot with both hands;
then, one should perform a swaying of the body in three directions.
Again, there is the striking against the waist with the throat-seal (kaṇṭhamudrā) well-stabilized;
having drawn back the movement by means of the wind, one performs the inhalation (pūraka) and the retention (kumbhaka). (38) Having placed both hands together and likewise both feet together—
One should pierce the four seats by means of the wind through the sequential yoga.
One should cause Great Meru to tremble with millions of winds, vajras, and fires.
Having pervaded both nostril-pouches, the wind vibrates swiftly.
One should indeed know the connection between the moon, the sun, and the fire for the sake of immortality;
once the state beyond death has arisen, whence can there be fear of death?
(41) This triad, possessing great qualities, is the destroyer of old age and death. (HP 3.29ab)
It is performed in eight ways, indeed, at every watch day after day;
it increases the fire [of vitality] and bestows the qualities such as *aṇimā*;
it always accumulates merit, destroys [the cycle of] rebirth, and shatters the flood of sins.
For those who possess the correct training, this initial practice is thus very slight:
at the outset, one should practice the avoidance of fire, women, and travel on roads.
Furthermore, there are the commencement, the pot, and the third, which is the conviction.
Accomplishment in all yogas consists of four stages of yoga:
(45) Through the piercing of the *brahmagranthi*, bliss arises from the void (*śūnya*);
within the body, the sound of the *nāda* is heard as a diverse resonance. (46)
Possessing a divine body, radiant, with a divine fragrance, free from disease, and full-hearted,
the yogin becomes heroic at the commencement [of practice].
(47) In the second [stage], having been brought to a state of equilibrium, the wind becomes centered in the middle.
The yogin should maintain a firm posture; through knowledge alone, he becomes equal in radiance.

Likewise, from the piercing of the Viṣṇu-knot, there arises an indication of supreme bliss. In the state of extreme emptiness (atiśūnya), there occurs the "crushing" (vimarda) and the sound of a kettledrum.
Then, on the third [day], having pierced through the maturation (*vipāka*), the sound of a drum arises in the sky;
at that time, the Great Void (*mahāśūnya*) is born, which is the support for all joints (*sarvasandhi*).
Then, having conquered the bliss of the mind (*cittānanda*), the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) comes into being.
Free from defects, death, old age, suffering, hunger, and sleep; then,
having pierced the Rudra-knot, the vital breath (anila), situated upon the seat of sattva,
becomes like the sound of a flute at its completion— a resonant sound that has transcended all resonance.
Then the mind becomes unified, designated as Rājayoga;
that [yogi] becomes equal to a Lord of Yogins, the agent of creation and dissolution. ||53||
Neither sound, nor the point (bindu), nor the mind, nor even the unconscious; there is nothing that cannot be overcome through practice—this is what is called Rājayoga. 54.
That in which the moving and the unmoving are dissolved by the power of dissolution is called the *liṅga*;
that is the Power (*śakti*) which, from its unfathomable depth of inconceivable form, illuminates the three worlds.

That indeed is meditation in which the mind is devoid of activity toward the objects of all things; that, O Kṣatriya, is meditation in which one effortlessly takes a seat for contemplation throughout the expanse of limitless time.
The body consists of the five elements and is filled with the five mandalas;
earth is to be known by its solidity, and water is that which has a liquid form. (56)
Light is the quality of fire, and likewise, touch belongs to air;
all consciousness resides in space—this is to be known by one who desires yoga. (57)
Twenty-one thousand six hundred and sixty breaths pass in a single day and night through the exhalation of the wind-mandala. (58)
When that orb of the earth has perished, the bodily strength of living beings comes to an end;
gradually their hair turns white, like blades of grass when the water has run dry. (59)
When the *tejas* is diminished, hunger and luster perish; when the *māruta* becomes slack, there is constant trembling, and one lives only through acts of daring.
Thus, from the destruction of [the elements] in this manner, death and life arise from the sustaining of the elements;
if one observes this for five hundred years, death will not occur otherwise. (61)
Through the practice performed for eight *yāmas*, he swallows all the breaths;
endowed with sixteen digits, that moon remains during the inhalations (*pūraka*).
When the mind is steady and free from waves, the vital air becomes centered within;
the sun (the solar channel) ascends to the upper station, and the bindu comes under control.
Filled with bliss, the yogi becomes like Śiva;
all the qualities of the Lord are seen [in him] after ten months. (64)
Thus, for the sake of the complete perfection of the host of immortals, this [work] has been revealed by Gorakṣa; it consists of the awakening to the skillful means of dissolution and so forth. 65.
Abandoning all thought, let this be examined for a single day;
if no conviction regarding that arises, then my words are indeed false. (66)
Like a mirage, a firefly, the flame of a lamp, the moon, and the sun—these [limited] portions manifest as the great image, the universal image. 67.
He who does not know awakening does not attain the host of immortals, even when equanimity has arisen in the mind that is free from duality. (68)
Having said, "I am," and "It is mine," one should contemplate the flood of immortals;
they say that the mind is life, and they know that the absence of mind is death. (69)
When the mind has become unmindful and equanimous, it is called liberation while living;
therein, the true nature of existence cannot even be described. //70//
Then no one lives, nor will anyone die;
having attained the state of Rājayoga, which brings all sentient beings under its control.

One may perform every action or not perform it at all, acting according to one's own inclination. In some places he is naked in caves; elsewhere he is clad in divine garments or a loincloth. In one place he is engaged in sexual union with celestial women; in another, he is a celibate student.
Delighting in subsisting on alms, he may at times obtain a place of enjoyment;
yet, with a conduct unattached everywhere, the king of yogis is the remover of all afflictions.
By the illustrious Lord Gorakṣanātha, who always dwells among the hosts of immortals,
the methods of dissolution (laya), mantra, and haṭha have been taught solely for the sake of Rājayoga.
One should examine with the body alone; what will mere eloquence of speech accomplish? What will merely reciting a medical treatise do for a patient? (74)
Thus ends the *Amarauṣhaprabodha*, composed by the illustrious Gorakṣanātha.
